name: Dusk
description: Eighties chorus polysynth for pads: one perfectly tuned oscillator per key with a locked sub octave, a four-pole filter that can sing, and a wide two-line stereo chorus.

params.name: Wave
params.description: Which waves the oscillator plays. Moving pulse slowly sweeps the width of the pulse, so even one held note keeps changing.

params.name: Sub
params.description: Level of the square wave an octave below the note. It is locked to the oscillator, so it adds weight without beating.

params.name: Low cut
params.description: Thins the low end in four steps, from the full sound to a light pad that leaves room for a bass.

params.name: Cutoff
params.description: Brightness of the low-pass filter. It follows the keyboard, so low and high notes keep the same colour.

params.name: Resonance
params.description: Emphasis at the cutoff. Higher makes the filter ring, and at the top it sings a pure note of its own that follows the keys.

params.name: Envelope
params.description: How far the envelope moves the filter. Above zero a note opens as it arrives and closes as it fades. Below zero it does the opposite.

params.name: Attack
params.description: How long a note takes to fade in. The filter moves with it, so a slow attack also blooms in brightness.

params.name: Release
params.description: How long a note takes to fade out after the key is let go. It also sets how quickly a held note settles from its peak.

params.name: Chorus
params.description: The stereo chorus. I is slow and calm, II is faster and deeper, I + II is a fast shimmer in the centre. Off is plain and mono.

params.name: Volume
params.description: Output level of the instrument. A soft clip after it rounds off the peaks when many notes stack up.

origin.note: Written for live-mix on cpp/kit. The signal path follows the Roland Juno-6, Juno-60 and Juno-106 in outline: one oscillator per voice whose sawtooth, pulse and sub-octave square share one phase, a four-position low cut on the sum of the voices, a four-pole low-pass with full keyboard follow that self-oscillates, one envelope for level and filter, and a stereo chorus of two delay lines moved by one triangle LFO in opposite polarity. It is not a circuit or sample emulation. Grounding: the Ambient Town instrument research (synthesizers, section 1), which rests on general knowledge and names the public chorus analysis by Andy Harman (pendragon-andyh/Juno60) as the place to verify its chorus figures; nothing was measured from a real instrument for this device. Design targets taken from that research: chorus I at 0.513 Hz and II at 0.863 Hz sweeping 1.66 to 5.35 ms, I + II at 9.75 Hz sweeping 3.3 to 3.7 ms with both sides in phase. Choices, not measurements of the original: low cut corners of 120, 350 and 800 Hz; the wet path's low-passes at 8 kHz; the hiss level (about -72 dBFS at the default volume); sustain fixed at 70 % with decay following release; the moving pulse at 0.6 Hz between 50 and 88 % width; an envelope depth of six octaves; resonance make-up of half the loss in decibels; attack extended to 8 s; ten voices instead of six. Simplified: no vibrato, noise source, range switch, gate mode, hold or arpeggiator; no bucket-brigade clock or saturation model in the chorus; the hiss stops when the instrument goes idle so the device can sleep, where the original hisses for as long as its chorus is on.
